details:
**Two heavy chains and two light chains (Y shape)**
Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins built from two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains held together by disulfide bridges. This structure is the most common giveaway for antibodies, which are also called immunoglobulins (Ig).

**Fab and Fc regions**
The two arms of the Y are the Fab (fragment antigen-binding) regions, whose variable tips each contain a paratope that binds an epitope on the antigen. The stem is the Fc (fragment crystallizable) region, a constant region that binds Fc receptors on immune cells and complement proteins; the arms and stem are joined by a flexible hinge region.

**Plasma cells (B cells)**
Antibodies are produced and secreted by plasma cells, which are activated B lymphocytes. They are the main effectors of humoral (antibody-mediated) adaptive immunity.

**V(D)J recombination**
The process that generates antibody diversity by randomly joining variable (V), diversity (D), and joining (J) gene segments, with D segments used only in heavy chains. It is carried out by the RAG-1 and RAG-2 recombinase proteins, adds extra N and P nucleotides at the junctions, and was discovered by Susumu Tonegawa. T cell receptors are formed by a closely related process.

**Monoclonal antibodies and hybridomas**
Monoclonal antibodies all come from one B cell clone and bind the same epitope. Georges Kohler and Cesar Milstein made them by fusing mouse spleen B cells with myeloma cells to form immortal hybridomas, selected in HAT medium (which contains aminopterin). Therapeutic monoclonals have names ending in "-mab," and mouse antibodies are "humanized" (pioneered by Greg Winter) to avoid the HAMA (human anti-mouse antibody) response.

**Isotypes: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD**
The five antibody classes, which differ in their heavy chain constant regions. IgG is the only one that crosses the placenta, IgA is dimeric and abundant in breast milk, IgM is pentameric and attacks foreign A and B blood group antigens, and IgE triggers histamine release from mast cells in allergic reactions.

**ELISA**
The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay detects and measures a target using antibodies linked to an enzyme. In a "sandwich" ELISA, a capture antibody binds the target and a detection antibody binds on top of it, producing a measurable signal.

**Western blot (primary and secondary antibodies)**
A technique for detecting a specific protein in a sample. A primary antibody binds the protein of interest, and a secondary antibody, often linked to horseradish peroxidase (HRP) or a fluorophore, binds the primary one for detection. Antibodies are similarly tagged with fluorophores in flow cytometry and indirect immunofluorescence.

**Somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation**
After an immune response begins, the variable region genes of antibodies are deliberately mutated at a high rate, and B cells producing higher-affinity antibodies are selected. This process, called affinity maturation, requires the enzyme activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID).

**Class switching**
Also called isotype switching or class switch recombination, this process changes which heavy chain constant region a B cell uses, converting, for example, IgM into IgG, without changing antigen specificity. It also requires activation-induced cytidine deaminase.

**Hypervariable regions (CDRs)**
The variable domain of each chain contains three hypervariable complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) set between four framework regions. The CDRs form loops that directly contact the antigen; antibody residues are numbered using the Kabat and Chothia schemes.

**Classical complement pathway and opsonization**
Antibodies bound to a target activate the classical complement pathway when C1q binds their Fc region, leading to C3 convertase and the membrane attack complex (MAC). Antibodies also act as opsonins, coating pathogens to enhance phagocytosis, and they cause agglutination and neutralization.

**Immunoglobulin fold**
Antibody domains consist of roughly 110-amino-acid repeats that fold into a "beta sandwich" of two beta sheets held together by a disulfide bond between cysteines. This fold is the defining feature of the immunoglobulin superfamily.

**Rheumatoid factor and autoantibodies**
Rheumatoid factor is an autoantibody that binds the Fc region of other antibodies and is associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Other disease-causing autoantibodies include thyroid-stimulating antibodies in Graves' disease and anti-dsDNA antibodies in lupus, detected using the kinetoplast of Crithidia luciliae.

**Rho(D) immune globulin and the Coombs test**
Anti-Rh antibodies, given as Rho(D) immune globulin to an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus, prevent her from becoming sensitized and causing hemolytic disease of the newborn. The direct Coombs test detects antibodies bound to red blood cells in such cases and in ABO incompatibility.
